content:
# Judith Chapter 8 — Disagreement Log
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
**Total Disagreements: 31**
Chapter 8 is the theological and literary centerpiece of the book. Judith enters the narrative as a widow of piety and beauty, then demolishes the elders' theological reasoning with precision and force. Disagreements are dense in her speech (vv. 11-27) and cluster around three concerns: (1) the register and intensity of her rebuke, (2) translation of key theological vocabulary (*boulai*, *hypotassein*, *peirazein*), and (3) the characterization of Judith herself in her introduction.

---

## Disagreements

**1. v. 1 — Narrative introduction**
- EMET: "And in those days Judith heard — she daughter of Merari..."
- LOGOS: "In those days Judith came to hear of it — Judith, daughter of Merari..."
- PNEUMA: "That is when Judith heard. Judith — daughter of Merari..."
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — most balanced between narrative smoothness and the appositive genealogy structure

**2. v. 3 — Death of Manasseh: "the heat fell upon his head"**
- EMET: "the heat fell upon his head"
- LOGOS: "the heat struck him on the head"
- PNEUMA: "the sun struck him on the head"
- SOPHIA ruling: "the heat struck him on the head" (LOGOS — *ho kauson* = the heat/scorching heat, not specifically "sun")

**3. v. 4 — "in her house"**
- EMET: "a widow in her house"
- LOGOS: "had lived as a widow in her house"
- PNEUMA: "had been a widow for" (drops "in her house")
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "in her house" is present in the Greek

**4. v. 7 — Beauty description (double formulation)**
- EMET: "very beautiful in appearance and comely-of-face"
- LOGOS: "very beautiful in appearance and exceedingly lovely to look upon"
- PNEUMA: "breathtakingly beautiful" (collapses both phrases into one)
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — both Greek phrases (*kalē tō eidei sphodra kai horaia tō prosōpō*) must be preserved

**5. v. 7 — "remained in these-things" / "remained the mistress"**
- EMET: "was-remaining in these-things"
- LOGOS: "remained the mistress of all these things"
- PNEUMA: "managed all of it herself, with full authority"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "mistress of all these things" supplies the implied authority clearly

**6. v. 8 — "feared God greatly"**
- EMET: "she feared God greatly"
- LOGOS: "she feared God exceedingly"
- PNEUMA: "she feared God with her whole being"
- SOPHIA ruling: "feared God exceedingly" (LOGOS — *sphodra* = exceedingly/greatly; PNEUMA adds "whole being" not in text)

**7. v. 9 — "evil words" / "harsh words"**
- EMET: "the evil words of the people"
- LOGOS: "the harsh words the people were speaking"
- PNEUMA: "what the people were saying against Uzziah — all the bitter complaints"
- SOPHIA ruling: "the harsh words the people were speaking" (LOGOS — *ponēra* can mean evil/harsh/bitter; "harsh" best suits public complaint)

**8. v. 9 — "fainthearted concerning the lack of water"**
- EMET: "because they were-fainthearted concerning the lack of water"
- LOGOS: "because they had lost heart over the lack of water"
- PNEUMA: "all the anger" (loses "fainthearted" language)
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "lost heart" renders *oligopsychia* (small-souledness)

**9. v. 11 — Opening address**
- EMET: "Hear me now, rulers of the inhabitants of Bethulia"
- LOGOS: "Listen to me, rulers of the people of Bethulia"
- PNEUMA: "Listen to me, rulers of Bethulia"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "rulers of the people of Bethulia" preserves the full Greek phrase

**10. v. 11 — "is not right" — the verdict on the oath**
- EMET: "is not right — this oath"
- LOGOS: "is not right — this oath"
- PNEUMA: "is wrong"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS/EMET — "is not right" is more precise than "is wrong"

**11. v. 12 — "who are you that you have tested God"**
- EMET: "who are you, that you have tested God today"
- LOGOS: "Who do you think you are, that you have put God to the test today"
- PNEUMA: "Who do you think you are, putting God to the test today?"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "put God to the test" is more precise than "tested God"; PNEUMA's rhetorical question form is also strong

**12. v. 12 — "set yourselves in the place of God"**
- EMET: "have set yourselves in-the-place of God among the children of men"
- LOGOS: "have set yourselves in God's place among human beings"
- PNEUMA: "Who appointed you to stand in God's place over your fellow human beings?"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — PNEUMA adds "appointed" and "over" not in the text

**13. v. 13 — "you will never understand anything"**
- EMET: "you will-never understand anything!"
- LOGOS: "you will never understand anything about him!"
- PNEUMA: "You will never understand him — not ever."
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — adds "about him" for clarity; PNEUMA's duplication is emphatic but not in Greek

**14. v. 14 — "plumb the depths of the heart"**
- EMET: "you cannot fathom the depth of the heart of a man"
- LOGOS: "you cannot plumb the depths of the human heart"
- PNEUMA: "You cannot even probe the depths of another human being's heart"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "plumb the depths" is more idiomatic English for *ereunēsete to bathos*

**15. v. 14 — "do not provoke... to anger" / "do not anger"**
- EMET: "do not provoke the Lord our God to anger"
- LOGOS: "do not anger the Lord our God"
- PNEUMA: "Do not make God angry"
- SOPHIA ruling: EMET/LOGOS blend: "do not provoke the Lord our God to anger" — *mē orgizete* is causative; LOGOS drops the causative

**16. v. 15 — "as many days as he pleases"**
- EMET: "in as-many days as he pleases"
- LOGOS: "within whatever days he pleases"
- PNEUMA: "on whatever timetable he chooses"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "within whatever days he pleases" is clearer than EMET's construction

**17. v. 16 — THE CENTRAL VERSE: "bind / pledge / lay pledges"**
- EMET: "Do not pledge-as-security the purposes of the Lord our God"
- LOGOS: "Do not lay pledges against the purposes of the Lord our God"
- PNEUMA: "Do not try to bind the purposes of the Lord our God"
- SOPHIA ruling: **PNEUMA** — "Do not try to bind the purposes of the Lord our God." The Greek *mē enechyrazetai* (from *enechyrazō* = to give as pledge/surety) carries the image of holding God's plans as collateral. PNEUMA's "bind" captures both the legal collateral sense and the broader theological point that God's freedom cannot be constrained. This is the most translation-significant ruling in the book.

**18. v. 16 — "like a man to be threatened"**
- EMET: "not like a man to be-threatened"
- LOGOS: "not like a man, to be coerced by threats"
- PNEUMA: "not a man you can bully"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "coerced by threats" is precise; PNEUMA's "bully" is colloquial

**19. v. 16 — "won over by pleading"**
- EMET: "nor like a son-of-man to be-prevailed-upon-by-entreaty"
- LOGOS: "nor like a human being, to be won over by pleading"
- PNEUMA: "not a person you can soften up with appeals"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — preserves the legal/diplomatic register of *hikanōthēsetai*

**20. v. 17 — "cry out" / "call on"**
- EMET: "let-us-call upon him to help us"
- LOGOS: "cry out to him to help us"
- PNEUMA: "cry out to him for help"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — *boēsōmen* = cry out; "call on" (EMET) is too mild

**21. v. 18 — "gods made by hands" / "gods made by human hands"**
- EMET: "gods made-by-hands"
- LOGOS: "gods made by human hands"
- PNEUMA: "handmade gods"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "made by human hands" is a standard biblical idiom worth preserving

**22. v. 19 — "fell with a great catastrophe"**
- EMET: "fell with a great catastrophe before our enemies"
- LOGOS: "fell with great ruin before their enemies"
- PNEUMA: "catastrophic defeat before their enemies"
- SOPHIA ruling: "fell with great catastrophe before their enemies" (EMET) — *ptōmati megalō* = great fall/catastrophe

**23. v. 21 — "require their blood from our mouths"**
- EMET: "he will require their blood from our mouths"
- LOGOS: "God will demand an accounting of their blood from us"
- PNEUMA: "God will hold us accountable for every drop of blood spilled"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "require their blood at our hands" — preserves blood-accountability idiom

**24. v. 22 — "offense and reproach"**
- EMET: "an-offense and a-reproach before those-who-acquired us"
- LOGOS: "an offense and a reproach in the eyes of those who enslave us"
- PNEUMA: "a disgrace and a shame to our captors"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "offense and reproach" matches the *oneidismon kai oneidos* pair; "those who enslave us" for *ktēsamenois*

**25. v. 24 — "demonstrate to our brothers"**
- EMET: "let-us-demonstrate to our brothers that their lives depend on us"
- LOGOS: "let us give our kindred this proof — that their very lives depend upon us"
- PNEUMA: "let us show our people what we are made of"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "give our kindred proof" renders *epideixōmetha* precisely

**26. v. 25 — "who is testing us"**
- EMET: "who is-testing us just as he-tested also our-fathers"
- LOGOS: "who is testing us even as he tested our ancestors"
- PNEUMA: "He is testing us, just as he tested our ancestors"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS phrasing; "ancestors" preferred over "fathers" for inclusive reading

**27. v. 27 — The furnace metaphor**
- EMET: "as they were in the furnace" (literal but opaque)
- LOGOS: "as if the fire were in their hearts" (explanatory paraphrase)
- PNEUMA: "send them into those fires to break them" (loose rendering)
- SOPHIA ruling: "as he refined them in the furnace" — introduces the refining metaphor explicitly to clarify the image

**28. v. 27 — "disciplines those who draw near"**
- EMET: "his hand disciplines those who draw near to him to admonish them"
- LOGOS: "his hand disciplines those who draw near to him, as a warning"
- PNEUMA: "he trains those who come close to him. He is shaping them, not crushing them"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — PNEUMA's "shaping them, not crushing them" is interpretive addition

**29. v. 31 — "devout woman"**
- EMET: "you are a-devout woman"
- LOGOS: "you are a devout woman"
- PNEUMA: "you are a woman of deep faith"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — *theosebēs* = god-fearing/devout; "devout" is standard

**30. v. 32 — "will go through" / "will be remembered"**
- EMET: "a thing that-will-go-through for the children of our race throughout all generations"
- LOGOS: "a thing that will be remembered among the children of our people for all generations"
- PNEUMA: "something that will echo through every generation of our people forever"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "will be remembered" is a reasonable interpretation of *dieleusetai* (lit. "will go through/pass through"); "echo" (PNEUMA) is too vivid

**31. v. 35 — "may the Lord God go before you for vengeance"**
- EMET: "may the Lord God go before you for-vengeance against our enemies"
- LOGOS: "may the Lord God go before you to take vengeance on our enemies"
- PNEUMA: "may the Lord God go ahead of you and bring vengeance on our enemies"
- SOPHIA ruling: LOGOS — "go before you to take vengeance" is most natural English; EMET's "for-vengeance" is awkward
